entries.name: Négritude
entries.desc: Négritude is a framework of critique and literary theory developed in the 1930s, mainly by French-speaking Black intellectuals and writers, to raise Black consciousness across Africa and its diaspora. Its founders included the Martinican poet Aimé Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor, later the first president of Senegal, and Léon Damas of French Guiana. Césaire first used the word in its present sense in 1935 in L'Étudiant noir, a magazine he had started in Paris with fellow students. Rejecting colonialism, racism and Eurocentrism, its writers drew on Marxism and Surrealism and celebrated African history and culture.

entries.name: Khilafat movement
entries.desc: The Khilafat movement was a political campaign of Muslims in British India against British policy towards Turkey and the planned dismemberment of the Ottoman Empire after the First World War. Its leaders, among them Abul Kalam Azad and the brothers Mohammad Ali Jauhar and Shaukat Ali, formed the All India Khilafat Committee to protect the caliphate. In 1920 they allied with Mahatma Gandhi and the Indian National Congress, and the Khilafatists became a major part of the Non-cooperation movement. Noted for promoting Hindu–Muslim unity, it faded after that campaign was called off in 1922, and Turkey's abolition of the caliphate in 1924 ended its cause.

entries.name: Kabir
entries.desc: Kabir was an Indian mystic poet and saint of Varanasi whose verses influenced the Bhakti movement; some historians place his life in 1398–1448, others in 1440–1518. A few accounts say he was raised by a Muslim weaver and his wife, and he is believed to have been a disciple of Ramananda. His songs and couplets, composed orally and gathered in collections such as the Bijak, attacked the hypocrisy and misguided rituals he saw in Hinduism and Islam alike. Verses attributed to him form the largest non-Sikh contribution to the Adi Granth.

entries.name: Andal
entries.desc: Andal was a Tamil poet-saint, probably of the 8th century, and the only woman among the twelve Alvars, the saints devoted to Vishnu in the Bhakti movement. Tradition holds that Periyalvar found her as a child under a tulasi plant at Srivilliputhur and that she would marry no one but Vishnu. She is credited with the Tiruppavai, 30 verses in which she imagines herself one of Krishna's cowherd girls, and the Nachiyar Tirumoli, about 140 verses of longing for Vishnu. Both are recited during the Tamil month of Margazhi, in December and January.

entries.name: Tulsidas
entries.desc: Tulsidas was a Hindu poet-saint of 16th-century northern India, devoted to the god Rama, who spent most of his life in Varanasi and Ayodhya. A Brahmin schooled in Sanskrit and the Vedas, he is best known for the Ramcharitmanas, a retelling of the Sanskrit Ramayana in the vernacular Awadhi, which he began at Ayodhya in 1574. Popular belief also makes him the author of the Hanuman Chalisa, and he is credited with founding the Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple in Varanasi and with starting the Ramlila plays, a folk-theatre version of the Ramayana.

entries.name: Tukaram
entries.desc: Tukaram was a 17th-century Marathi poet-saint of the Varkari tradition, born at Dehu in Maharashtra and devoted to the god Vithoba, a form of Vishnu. In his abhangas, devotional poems in a simple folk style, he attacked caste hierarchy, mechanical ritual and the misconduct of certain religious leaders, which brought him opponents such as a local monastery head, Mambaji Gosavi. Tradition credits him with some 4,500 abhangas, collected in the Tukaram Gatha, whose manuscripts were reworked for about two centuries after his death. Among his disciples was a Brahmin woman, Bahinabai.

credit.artist: Anant Shivaji Desai, Ravi Varma Press

entries.name: Namdev
entries.desc: Namdev was a Marathi poet-saint of the Varkari tradition and a devotee of the god Vithoba of Pandharpur; tradition dates his life to 1270–1350, but scholars have proposed dates from the 13th to the 15th century. Born into a caste of tailors, he composed simply worded songs of praise and taught that all could be saved by devotion, without regard to caste. His companions in worship included Gora, a potter, Janabai, a maid, and Chokhamela, of a caste treated as untouchable. Sixty-one songs under his name are in the Adi Granth, the Sikh scripture.

entries.name: Ravidas
entries.desc: Ravidas was an Indian mystic poet-saint of the Bhakti movement who lived in the 15th and 16th centuries, though the details of his life are uncertain. Born near Varanasi to parents of the leather-working Chamar caste, treated as untouchable, he taught the removal of divisions of caste and gender and worshipped God as nirguna, without attributes. Forty-one of his poems are in the Adi Granth, the Sikh scripture, and tradition names the Rajput princess Mirabai as his disciple. He is the central figure of the Ravidassia religious movement.

entries.name: Rifa'a al-Tahtawi
entries.desc: Rifa'a al-Tahtawi was a 19th-century Egyptian writer, teacher and translator, an early figure of the Nahda, the Arab renaissance. A scholar of al-Azhar, he went to Paris in 1826 as imam to a student mission sent by Muhammad Ali and read Voltaire, Rousseau and Montesquieu there; his account of France, Takhlis al-ibriz fi talkhis Bariz, appeared in 1834. In 1835 he founded the School of Languages in Cairo, and he supervised the translation of more than 2,000 foreign works into Arabic. His guide to educating girls and boys alike was published in 1873.

credit.artist: The original uploader was Zerida at English Wikipedia.

entries.name: Butrus al-Bustani
entries.desc: Butrus al-Bustani was a writer and scholar from Mount Lebanon, a major figure of the Nahda, the Arab renaissance. Born a Maronite, he became a Protestant while working for American missionaries in Beirut and helped translate the Bible into Arabic. After the 1860 civil war his Nafir Suriyya, the Clarion of Syria, appealed for unity in a Syrian homeland, and in 1863 he founded the secular National School in Beirut, open to all religions. He compiled the dictionary Muhit al-Muhit, founded the journal al-Jinan in 1870 and in 1876 began the encyclopedia Da'irat al-Ma'arif.

entries.name: Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq
entries.desc: Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq was an Ottoman scholar, writer and journalist from Mount Lebanon, considered one of the founding fathers of modern Arabic literature. Born a Maronite, he became a Protestant in Egypt, where he lived from 1825, and from 1848 worked in England on an Arabic translation of the Bible, published in 1857. In Paris in 1855 he published al-Saq 'ala al-saq, a long, digressive novel drawing on his own life. In 1860 he converted to Islam, taking the name Ahmad, and in 1861 he founded the Arabic newspaper al-Jawa'ib in Istanbul.

entries.name: Muhammad Abduh
entries.desc: Muhammad Abduh was an Egyptian Islamic scholar, judge and reformer, a central figure of the Nahda and of Islamic modernism. A disciple of Jamal al-Din al-Afghani from his student years at al-Azhar, he argued that Muslims must use reason rather than simply rely on medieval interpretations of the texts. Exiled in 1882 for supporting the Urabi revolt, he published the journal al-'Urwa al-wuthqa with al-Afghani in Paris in 1884. After his return in 1888 he became a judge, and from 1899 until his death he was Grand Mufti of Egypt.

credit.artist: The original uploader was Zerida at English Wikipedia.

entries.name: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani
entries.desc: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani was a political activist and Islamic thinker who travelled across the Muslim world in the late 19th century, one of the founders of Islamic modernism. He claimed Afghan origin, but several scholars hold that he was born into a Shia family in Asadabad, Iran. In Cairo he gained a disciple, Muhammad Abduh, with whom he published the journal al-'Urwa al-wuthqa in Paris in 1884, calling for unity among Muslims. He was implicated in the plot of his follower Mirza Reza Kermani, who shot Naser al-Din Shah of Iran in 1896.

credit.artist: Yacquub cAbd al-cAziiz Abul Ala Maududi

entries.name: Qasim Amin
entries.desc: Qasim Amin was an Egyptian jurist and Islamic modernist, a co-founder of Cairo University and often counted among the Arab world's first feminists. Born in Alexandria, he took a law degree in Egypt and studied at Montpellier in France, and from 1885 served in Egypt's courts. He criticised veiling, seclusion, early marriage and the lack of education for women, and his book The Liberation of Women, published in 1899, called for an end to the veil. His advocacy stirred debate across the Arab world, though scholars such as Leila Ahmed have questioned his feminism.

entries.name: Jurji Zaydan
entries.desc: Jurji Zaydan was a Lebanese novelist, journalist and teacher of the Nahda who settled in Cairo and founded the magazine al-Hilal there in 1892. Born in Beirut to an Orthodox Christian family, he studied medicine at the Syrian Protestant College before moving to Egypt. His historical novels, about one a year from 1891 and serialised in al-Hilal, aimed to teach ordinary Arabs their own history. His secular History of Islamic Civilisation, published from 1901 to 1906, was controversial, and in 1910 public objections cost him a chair at the new Egyptian University.

entries.name: Prince Gong
entries.desc: Yixin, Prince Gong, was a Qing imperial prince and statesman, the sixth son of the Daoguang Emperor and a leader of China's Self-Strengthening Movement. Left behind with full powers when the Xianfeng Emperor fled Beijing in 1860, he signed the Convention of Peking with the British, French and Russians. In 1861 he set up the Zongli Yamen, in effect a foreign ministry, and joined the Empresses Dowager Ci'an and Cixi in a coup against the late emperor's regents, serving as prince-regent until 1865. Cixi dismissed him in 1884 and recalled him in 1894.

entries.name: Wenxiang
entries.desc: Wenxiang was a Manchu statesman of China's Qing dynasty, a bannerman of the Plain Red Banner, and one of the architects of the Self-Strengthening Movement. After gaining the jinshi, the highest degree of the imperial examination, in 1845, he joined the Grand Council in 1858. When the Xianfeng Emperor fled Beijing during the Second Opium War, he stayed and took part in the negotiations with the British and French. A founder of the Zongli Yamen, he was instrumental in devising the government's policy of cooperation with the Western powers between 1861 and 1876.

entries.name: Zhang Zhidong
entries.desc: Zhang Zhidong was a Chinese official of the late Qing dynasty who advocated controlled reform and the modernisation of the army, serving as viceroy of Huguang from 1889. He ordered an iron and steel plant from England, which began production in 1894 but made substantial losses, and founded a mint, mills and factories. His Exhortation to Study of 1898 summed up his relatively conservative reform in the phrase "Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for application". He took a leading role in abolishing the imperial examination in 1905.

entries.name: Yung Wing
entries.desc: Yung Wing was a Chinese-American diplomat and businessman who in 1854 became the first recorded Chinese graduate of an American university, Yale College. In 1863 Zeng Guofan sent him to the United States to buy machinery, which went into the Jiangnan Arsenal at Shanghai. He persuaded the Qing government to send young students abroad and organised the Chinese Educational Mission, which brought 120 of them to New England from 1872 until it was disbanded in 1881. A naturalised American citizen from 1852, he lost that status under the Chinese Exclusion Act.

entries.name: Zongli Yamen
entries.desc: The Zongli Yamen was the office in charge of foreign policy in China under the late Qing dynasty, set up by Prince Gong in 1861 after the Convention of Peking. Before it, foreign relations had been handled by several agencies, among them the Ministry of Rites and the Lifan Yuan. It was supervised by five senior officials, at first all Manchus, with Prince Gong as their leader in practice, and from 1875 it opened legations and consulates abroad. The Boxer Protocol of 1901 replaced it with a Foreign Office, the Waiwubu.

entries.name: Tongwen Guan
entries.desc: The Tongwen Guan, or School of Combined Learning, was a government school of Western languages and science founded at Beijing in 1862 to train interpreters for the Zongli Yamen. It opened with ten students of English; a proposal to add astronomy and mathematics was opposed by conservatives led by Woren, who feared "learning from foreigners". By 1877, with W. A. P. Martin as dean, it taught foreign languages and subjects from chemistry to international law to over a hundred students. In 1902 it was absorbed into the Imperial University of Peking, now Peking University.

entries.name: Jiangnan Arsenal
entries.desc: The Jiangnan Arsenal was a state-owned arms factory and shipyard at Shanghai, planned under Zeng Guofan and set up by Li Hongzhang in 1865 during the Self-Strengthening Movement. It combined a plant bought from an American firm, the assets of the Suzhou and Anqing arsenals and machinery Yung Wing bought in the United States. The largest of the movement's arsenals, it built its first steamship, the Huiji, in 1868 and ran a language school and a translation house. Its shipyard, split off in 1905, survives as the Jiangnan Shipyard; its arms works closed in 1937.

entries.name: Fuzhou Navy Yard
entries.desc: The Fuzhou Navy Yard, or Foochow Arsenal, was a shipyard at Mawei in Fuzhou prefecture, created by the Qing Empire with French help during the Self-Strengthening Movement. Planned from 1866 under Zuo Zongtang with a naval college, it was built from 1867 under the French naval officers Prosper Giquel and Paul d'Aiguebelle, contracted to provide within five years a dockyard, eleven transports, five gunboats and schools of navigation and marine engineering. Its first ship, the Wannian Qing, was launched in June 1869. French forces severely damaged the yard during the Sino-French War in 1884.

entries.name: Beiyang Fleet
entries.desc: The Beiyang Fleet, or Northern Ocean Fleet, was one of four regional navies of late Qing China, sponsored by Li Hongzhang to guard the approaches to Beijing. Begun in 1871 and equipped mostly with warships built in Germany and Britain, among them the battleships Dingyuan and Zhenyuan, it was the largest fleet in Asia in the late 1880s. In 1888 it was formally placed under the Navy Yamen, and its budget was cut. Under Ding Ruchang it suffered heavy losses at the Battle of the Yalu River in 1894 and was annihilated at Weihaiwei.

entries.name: Robert Hart
entries.desc: Sir Robert Hart was a British official serving Qing China, the second inspector-general of its Imperial Maritime Customs Service, which he headed for over four decades from 1863. Born in Portadown, Ireland, he came to China in 1854 as a student interpreter and joined the customs at Canton in 1859. Responsible for collecting customs duties for the Chinese government, he extended the service to more ports, standardised its work and insisted on efficiency and honesty; a modern postal service was later added. In 1862 he helped Prince Gong set up the Tongwen Guan.

entries.name: Stone tools
entries.desc: Stone tools are implements shaped from stone by knapping or grinding; the oldest known, from Lomekwi near Lake Turkana in Kenya, are dated to 3.3 million years ago, about a million years before the genus Homo. The earliest known Oldowan tools, from Nyayanga in Kenya, date to about 2.9 million years ago, and the Acheulean industry, best known for its hand axes, appears in the West Turkana area by 1.7 million years ago. Polished stone axes were important for clearing woods and forests in the Neolithic and were traded over long distances.

entries.name: Control of fire
entries.desc: The control of fire by early humans gave warmth, light, protection from predators and a means of cooking; the earliest known controlled use of fire took place in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, 1.79–1.0 million years ago. Heated fish teeth at the Daughters of Jacob Bridge in the Golan Heights, about 780,000 years ago, are the oldest likely evidence of cooking. The oldest definitive evidence of fire-making, about 400,000 years ago, comes from a Neanderthal site in eastern England, where burnt soil was found with flint handaxes and iron pyrite used to strike sparks.

entries.name: Pottery
entries.desc: Pottery is the craft and products of forming vessels and other objects from clay fired at high temperatures; the earliest known pottery vessels, from Xianren Cave in Jiangxi, China, date to 20,000–19,000 years ago. Ceramic figurines are older: the Venus of Dolní Věstonice in the Czech Republic is dated to 29,000–25,000 BCE. Pottery appears to have been developed independently in sub-Saharan Africa, where finds in Mali date to at least 9,400 BCE, and in South America. Durable pottery sherds are typically the most common artefacts to survive on archaeological sites.

entries.name: Potter's wheel
entries.desc: The potter's wheel is a machine for shaping, or throwing, clay into round ceramic ware; the oldest found, from the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture in western Ukraine, dates to the middle of the 5th millennium BCE. Slow wheels (tournettes) were in use in the Near East around 3500 BCE; the fast wheel, which made throwing possible, followed in the mid to late 3rd millennium BCE. Throwing allowed thinner walls, more varied shapes and many more pots per hour. The wheel became widespread throughout the Old World but was unknown in the pre-Columbian Americas.

entries.name: Copper smelting
entries.desc: Copper smelting is the production of copper from its ores at high temperature; the world's oldest securely dated evidence for it, from c. 5000 BCE, was found at Belovode on Rudnik mountain in Serbia. The Chalcolithic, or Copper Age, between the Neolithic and the Bronze Age, was characterised by the increasing use of smelted copper, although stone tools still predominated. Andean civilisations appear to have invented copper smelting independently, and it developed independently in the Aïr Mountains of Niger between 3000 and 2500 BCE.

entries.name: Glassblowing
entries.desc: Glassblowing is the technique of inflating molten glass into a bubble with a blowpipe and shaping it, developed by Phoenician and Syrian craftsmen in the 1st century BCE, in what are now Lebanon and Israel. It quickly eclipsed casting and core-forming, spreading with the Roman Empire to workshops in Italy, the Rhineland and beyond. Mould-blowing, introduced in the 1st century CE, allowed glass vessels to be made quickly in large quantities. Free-blowing remained the leading way of forming glass until the late 19th century.

entries.name: Cast iron
entries.desc: Cast iron is an iron–carbon alloy with more than 2% carbon, valued for its relatively low melting temperature; the earliest known cast-iron artefacts, from what is now Jiangsu in China, date to the 8th century BCE. Its production became widespread in China by about the 5th century BCE, and blast furnaces allowed the mass production of cast-iron agricultural tools. Burgundy used it for cannons and shot in the 15th century, and from the late 1770s, when Abraham Darby III built the Iron Bridge in Shropshire, it was used for bridges and buildings.

entries.name: Crucible steel
entries.desc: Crucible steel is steel made by melting iron, often with fluxes, in a crucible, which allows precise control of its carbon content; it was first developed in southern India and Sri Lanka by the wootz process, with material as early as 300 BCE. Wootz steel was traded widely and became famous in the Middle East as Damascus steel. In England, Benjamin Huntsman of Sheffield developed it in parallel from 1740, making the first fully homogeneous steel; within a century Sheffield's output rose from about 200 to over 80,000 tonnes a year.

entries.name: Bessemer process
entries.desc: The Bessemer process makes steel from molten pig iron by blowing air through it to burn off excess carbon and other impurities; it was patented by the Englishman Henry Bessemer in 1856. It was the first inexpensive industrial process for mass-producing steel, converting three to five tons of iron in 10 to 20 minutes rather than at least a full day. By cutting the cost of steel from £40 to £6–7 per long ton, it made steel about as cheap as wrought iron, and railways in particular turned to steel.

entries.name: Spinning wheel
entries.desc: The spinning wheel is a device in which a hand- or foot-turned wheel drives the spindle that spins fibres into thread or yarn; its origin is disputed, and some scholars hold that Chinese dictionaries of the 2nd century CE mention it. Others place its invention in India or the Middle East, where evidence points to it being known by 1030; the earliest clear illustration was drawn in Baghdad in 1237. It spread from the Middle East to Europe by the 13th century and raised the productivity of thread-making more than tenfold.

entries.name: Spinning jenny
entries.desc: The spinning jenny is a multi-spindle spinning frame invented in 1764–1765 by James Hargreaves at Stanhill, Oswaldtwistle, in Lancashire, England. One worker could work eight or more spools at once, a number that later grew to 120, which helped meet the weavers' demand for yarn after the flying shuttle. Hargreaves patented it in 1770; it produced coarse thread and was superseded by the spinning mule, but it helped start the factory system of cotton manufacturing.

entries.name: Jacquard machine
entries.desc: The Jacquard machine is a device fitted to a loom that automates the weaving of complex patterns such as brocade and damask, controlled by a chain of punched cards; it was patented by Joseph Marie Jacquard in 1804. It built on earlier inventions by Basile Bouchon, Jean Baptiste Falcon and Jacques Vaucanson, and made possible the automatic production of unlimited varieties of complex patterns. Its use of replaceable punched cards to control a sequence of operations inspired Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and is considered an important step in the history of computing.

entries.name: Cotton gin
entries.desc: The cotton gin is a machine that separates cotton fibres from their seeds; the earliest evidence of it is a single-roller gin depicted in 5th-century Buddhist paintings in the Ajanta Caves in western India. Two-roller gins appeared in India and China between the 12th and 14th centuries, and the Indian worm-gear roller gin is still in use. In 1793 the American Eli Whitney created a mechanical gin for short-staple cotton, patented in 1794; it made cotton farming more profitable and increased the demand for enslaved labour in the American South.

entries.name: Bakelite
entries.desc: Bakelite is a hard phenol formaldehyde resin, the first plastic made from synthetic components, developed by the chemist Leo Baekeland in Yonkers, New York, in 1907 and patented in 1909. Because it could be moulded into any shape and is heat-resistant and electrically non-conductive, it was used for electrical insulators, radio and telephone casings, kitchenware, jewellery and toys. Its commercial success led to other synthetic plastics, and the American Chemical Society named it a National Historic Chemical Landmark as the world's first commercial synthetic plastic.

credit.artist: Original uploader was Robneild at en.wikipedia

entries.name: Eyeglasses
entries.desc: Eyeglasses, or spectacles, are lenses held in a frame in front of the eyes; the first are estimated to have been made in central Italy, most likely in Pisa or Florence, by about 1290. In a sermon of 23 February 1306 the Dominican friar Giordano da Pisa said the art had been found less than twenty years before. Venice soon became a centre of manufacture using Murano glass, and by 1301 guild regulations there governed their sale. The earliest surviving examples, found at Kloster Wienhausen in Germany, date from about 1400.

entries.name: Neolithic Revolution
entries.desc: The Neolithic Revolution, or First Agricultural Revolution, was the transition of many human cultures from hunting and gathering to farming and settlement, which began in the Fertile Crescent between 10,000 and 8000 BCE. Farming also arose separately in other regions, among them China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica and three areas of Africa. Surplus food supported denser settlements and specialised labour, and provided the basis for centralised administrations and writing. Diets narrowed, however, and studies find that people grew shorter after the transition.

credit.artist: Iris Groman-Yaroslavski , Ehud Weiss, Dani Nadel

entries.name: Domestication
entries.desc: Domestication is a long-term relationship in which one species takes over the control and care of another to obtain resources such as meat, milk or labour; domestication by humans began with the dog at least 15,000 years ago. Plant domestication began with wheat and barley in the Middle East around 13,000–11,000 years ago, and goats, pigs, sheep and cattle were domesticated in the Fertile Crescent 11,000–10,000 years ago. Agriculture developed in some 13 centres, each domesticating different crops and animals. Domesticated mammals tend to be smaller and less aggressive than their wild ancestors.

entries.name: Irrigation
entries.desc: Irrigation is the practice of applying controlled amounts of water to land to help grow crops, with some of the earliest known use dating to the 6th millennium BCE in Khuzistan, south-west Iran. Choga Mami in Iraq is believed to show the first canal irrigation, at about 6000 BCE; the earliest known canals in the Americas, in Peru's Zaña Valley, date to at least 3400 BCE. Egyptians let the Nile flood into basins enclosed by dykes, and China's Dujiangyan system, built in 256 BCE, still supplies water.

credit.artist: Photography: Barbara Steinemann Derivative work: Zacharie Grossen

entries.name: Plough
entries.desc: A plough is a farm tool for loosening or turning soil before sowing; ploughs were at first powered by people, and the larger ox-drawn ard, or scratch plough, followed the domestication of oxen in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, perhaps as early as the 6th millennium BCE. A ploughed field from c. 2800 BCE has been found at Kalibangan in India. Han China made the earliest known heavy iron mould-board ploughs, and in Europe the general adoption of the heavy plough seems to have accompanied the three-field system in the 8th–9th centuries.

entries.name: Andén
entries.desc: An andén (plural andenes) is a stair-step terrace dug into a hillside for farming, built by pre-Columbian cultures in the Andes by 2000 BCE. Layers of stone, gravel and topsoil behind stone retaining walls drained the soil, while the walls stored the sun's heat against frost; one aim was to grow maize up to 3,500 metres. Under the Inca Empire andenes covered an estimated 1,000,000 hectares, and many are still farmed after more than 500 years.

entries.name: Seed drill
entries.desc: A seed drill is a device that sows seeds by placing them in the soil at a set depth; the Babylonians used primitive seed drills around 1400 BCE. The Chinese invented multi-tube iron seed drills in the 2nd century BCE. In Europe the first known seed drill was patented in Venice in 1566 and Jethro Tull refined it in 1701, but drills spread widely only in the mid to late 19th century. A seed drill can raise the yield per seed planted as much as eightfold compared with broadcasting by hand.

credit.artist: Sung Ying Hsing. Reference "Chinese technology in the 17th century"

entries.name: Three-field system
entries.desc: The three-field system is a crop rotation in which a field bears one set of crops in the first year, another in the second, and lies fallow in the third; it was first used in China in the Eastern Zhou period. It arose independently in medieval Europe, where it replaced the two-field system, which left half the land fallow, between the 9th and 11th centuries. Legumes such as peas and beans restored nitrogen to the soil, and its introduction coincided with the adoption of the mould-board plough.

entries.name: Horse collar
entries.desc: A horse collar is a padded harness collar that spreads a load across a horse's shoulders and chest without pressing on its windpipe; it was invented in China by the early medieval period. The earliest certain depiction is a Dunhuang cave mural of 477–499 CE, from the Northern Wei dynasty. It spread westward and was clearly in use in Europe by 1000, where horses came to be used more widely for ploughing, working roughly 50 per cent faster than oxen.

entries.name: Beer
entries.desc: Beer is one of the oldest human-produced drinks, made by fermenting cereal grains; the earliest archaeological evidence of fermentation is 13,000-year-old residues of a gruel-like beer used by the Natufians for ritual feasting at Raqefet Cave, in present-day Israel. The first written records of brewing come from Mesopotamia, where a Sumerian poem to the brewing goddess Ninkasi, about 3,900 years old, holds the oldest surviving beer recipe. Hops, known from at least the 9th century, made beer keep and turned brewing in late medieval northern Europe into an export industry.

credit.artist: Ur-Amma, the scribe who created the text, Dr Tom L. Lee who photographed it, SilkTork who created the image.

entries.name: Refrigeration
entries.desc: Refrigeration is the artificial cooling of a space, substance or system below the surrounding temperature; the harvesting of snow and ice is estimated to have begun before 1000 BCE, and artificial refrigeration began with a small machine designed by William Cullen in 1755. Jacob Perkins built the first working vapour-compression system in 1834, and James Harrison, whose ice-making machine at Geelong, Victoria, dates from 1851, built the first practical one. Refrigerated ships carried frozen meat from New Zealand to Britain from 1882, and by 1940 more than half of American households owned a refrigerator.

entries.name: Mudbrick
entries.desc: A mudbrick is an air-dried, unfired brick of mud mixed with a binder such as straw or rice husks, first known from the dwellings of Jericho, dated to 9000 BCE. Sun-dried mudbricks were the most common construction material in pharaonic Egypt, and people at Mehrgarh in South Asia lived in mudbrick houses between 7000 and 3300 BCE. From around 5000–4000 BCE they evolved into fired bricks, but they remain standard in vernacular building in parts of Africa and western Asia. The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali is the world's largest mudbrick structure.

entries.name: Arch
entries.desc: An arch is a curved structure spanning an opening, bearing the load above it or serving as decoration, first known in the ancient Near East, where the Nippur arch was built before 3800 BCE. There it was used rarely, mostly underground in structures such as drains, where sideways thrust is much reduced. The Romans, who learned the semicircular arch from the Etruscans, were the first builders in Europe to use its full potential above ground, in bridges, aqueducts and the Colosseum. Wrought iron and steel reduced its structural role from the mid-19th century.

entries.name: Roman concrete
entries.desc: Roman concrete, or opus caementicium, is a building material used in ancient Rome: a hydraulic-setting cement mixed with an aggregate, in widespread use from about 150 BCE. The Romans first used it in coastal underwater structures, probably in the harbours around Baiae before the end of the 2nd century BCE, and around 25 BCE Vitruvius recommended volcanic pozzolana for structural mortars. Its aggregates often included larger pieces than modern concrete, so it was laid rather than poured. The dome of the Pantheon, the world's largest and oldest unreinforced concrete dome, is built of it.

entries.name: Dome
entries.desc: A dome is an architectural element resembling the hollow upper half of a sphere; the earliest found may be four dwellings of mammoth tusks and bones at Mezhirich in Ukraine, dated between 19,280 and 11,700 BCE. Corbelled stone domes appear in the Neolithic Near East, and domes were built in ancient Mesopotamia and in Persian, Hellenistic, Roman and Chinese architecture. They reached monumental size in the Roman Imperial period, whose largest dome is the Pantheon, and were later common in Byzantine, Islamic, Renaissance and Ottoman architecture.

entries.name: Inca rope bridge
entries.desc: Inca rope bridges are simple suspension bridges of woven grass that the Inca Empire built over canyons, gorges and rivers as part of its road system. Since the Incas did not use wheeled transport, the bridges carried pedestrians, livestock and the chasqui runners who delivered messages. Local villagers replaced each cable every year as part of their mit'a public service, dangerous work in which repairers often faced death. The last remaining one, the Q'iswa Chaka over the Apurímac River near Huinchiri in Peru, is still rebuilt by local residents every June.

entries.name: Pound lock
entries.desc: A pound lock is a chamber with gates at both ends in which the water level is raised or lowered to move boats between levels of a waterway, first built in Song dynasty China by Qiao Weiyue in 984. He placed two sluice gates 250 feet apart under a roof, replacing double slipways, at one of which soldiers had plotted with bandits to wreck grain barges. On the Grand Canal such locks raised the water level by 138 feet. The first true European pound lock was built at Damme near Bruges in 1396.

entries.name: Anji Bridge
entries.desc: The Anji Bridge, or Zhaozhou Bridge, is a stone bridge over the Xiaohe River in Zhao County, Hebei, built in 595–605 under the Sui dynasty and credited to the craftsman Li Chun; it is the world's oldest open-spandrel segmental arch bridge of stone. Its shallow arch spans 37.37 metres and saves about 40 per cent of the material a semicircular arch would need. Two small arches at each end lighten it and let floodwater through. It is the oldest standing bridge in China and influenced later Chinese bridges.

entries.name: Stepwell
entries.desc: A stepwell, or vav, is a well, cistern or pond reached by a long corridor of steps down to the water, developed in India, where the earliest archaeological evidence is at Dholavira. Ashoka's inscriptions describe stepwells dug along major roads as an established practice of earlier kings, and the first rock-cut examples date from 200–400 CE. Built in south-western Gujarat around 600 CE, they spread north to Rajasthan, and their construction peaked under Muslim rule from the 11th to the 16th century. Lined with unmortared stone, they gave year-round access to groundwater.

entries.name: Elevator
entries.desc: An elevator, or lift, is a machine that carries people or goods vertically between levels; the earliest known reference, by the Roman architect Vitruvius, reports that Archimedes built one, probably in 236 BCE. The Colosseum, completed in 80 CE, had about 25 elevators powered by men for raising animals. Steam-powered elevators served mines and factories in the mid-19th century, and in 1852 Elisha Otis introduced the safety elevator, which kept the cab from falling if the cable broke; the first passenger one was installed in New York City in 1857.

entries.name: Skyscraper
entries.desc: A skyscraper is a very tall building, typically defined as at least 150 metres high, of a type that first emerged in the United States in the late 19th century; many regard the ten-storey Home Insurance Building in Chicago, built in 1884–1885, as the first. Its architect, William Le Baron Jenney, made a steel frame carry the whole weight of the walls, and the building also used elevators, fireproofing and electrical wiring. Construction surged in the 1960s and boomed in East and Southeast Asia in the 1990s; over 7,000 now exceed 150 metres.

entries.name: Water wheel
entries.desc: A water wheel is a machine that turns the energy of flowing or falling water into power through a large wheel with blades or buckets on its rim; it first appeared in ancient Egypt in the 4th century BCE, where wheels lifted water for irrigation. By the 3rd century BCE they turned millstones in the Near East, and in China from 31 CE they drove blast-furnace bellows for cast iron. They supplied power for the Industrial Revolution until the turbine of Benoît Fourneyron, whose first model dates from 1827, began to displace them.

entries.name: Windmill
entries.desc: A windmill is a machine driven by wind acting on vanes or sails to grind grain or pump water, first known in Persia, where windmills were working in Khorasan in the 9th century. These had sails turning around a vertical shaft and spread across the Middle East and Central Asia, reaching southern Europe by the 11th century. The vertical windmill developed in north-western Europe in the 12th century, and the earliest certain reference to one in northern Europe dates from 1185, at Weedley in Yorkshire. Europe's windmills peaked at about 200,000 around 1850.

entries.name: Aeolipile
entries.desc: An aeolipile, or Hero's engine, is a simple bladeless steam turbine, a vessel that spins as steam escapes through bent nozzles, described by Hero of Alexandria in the 1st century CE and usually credited to him. Vitruvius mentioned aeolipiles in his De architectura of about 30–20 BCE, and both men drew on the earlier work of Ctesibius in Alexandria. Considered the first recorded steam engine, it is neither a practical source of power nor a direct ancestor of the Industrial Revolution's steam engines.

entries.name: Steam engine
entries.desc: A steam engine is a heat engine that does mechanical work with steam, usually by pushing a piston in a cylinder; the Spanish inventor Jerónimo de Ayanz patented the first steam-powered water pump, for draining mines, in 1606. Thomas Savery's pump of 1698 was the first commercial steam-powered device, and Thomas Newcomen's engine of about 1712 the first commercially successful one to transmit continuous power to a machine. From 1763 James Watt improved it with a separate condenser, greatly cutting fuel use, and by the 19th century steam engines powered factories, railways and ships.

entries.name: Electric generator
entries.desc: An electric generator is a machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy; the first electromagnetic generator, the Faraday disk, was built by the British scientist Michael Faraday in 1831, a copper disc turning between the poles of a horseshoe magnet. Dynamos, which produce direct current through a commutator, followed from 1832, and the Woolrich generator of 1844 was the earliest used in industry, for electroplating. Self-excited dynamos, invented independently by Wheatstone, Siemens and Varley in 1866–1867, made high power generation possible, and generators now produce nearly all grid electricity.

entries.name: Internal combustion engine
entries.desc: An internal combustion engine is a heat engine in which fuel burns with air or another oxidiser inside the engine, and the expanding gases push directly on pistons, turbine blades, a rotor or a nozzle; Robert Street patented one in 1794. In 1807 Nicéphore and Claude Niépce's Pyréolophore, fired by dust explosions, powered a boat on the Saône in France. Commercially successful engines followed in the mid-19th century, and Nicolaus Otto's four-stroke engine of 1876 was the first modern one. They are now the main power source of cars, aircraft and boats.

entries.name: Incandescent light bulb
entries.desc: An incandescent light bulb is an electric light in which current heats a filament until it glows inside an evacuated or gas-filled glass bulb; Humphry Davy made an electric incandescent light in 1802 at the Royal Institution of Great Britain. Many experimenters followed, and from 1878 Joseph Swan in Britain and Thomas Edison developed practical carbon-filament bulbs: Edison's first successful test, on 22 October 1879, lasted 13.5 hours, and Swan's bulbs were in daily use in London in 1881. Tungsten filaments, patented in Hungary in 1904, gave brighter, longer-lasting light.

entries.name: Steam turbine
entries.desc: A steam turbine is a heat engine that extracts energy from pressurised steam to turn a rotating shaft; Taqi al-Din described one that turned a spit in Ottoman Egypt in 1551, after the aeolipile of Hero of Alexandria. Its modern form was invented by Charles Parsons in 1884: his first model was connected to a dynamo generating 7.5 kilowatts, and his turbine made cheap and plentiful electricity possible and changed marine transport and naval warfare. Steam turbines generated about 42 per cent of the United States' electricity in 2022.

entries.name: Oil well
entries.desc: An oil well is a hole bored into the Earth to bring petroleum to the surface; the earliest known were drilled in China in 347 CE. They were drilled with bits attached to bamboo poles to depths of up to about 240 metres, and their oil was burned to evaporate brine and produce salt. The first modern oil wells were drilled on the Absheron Peninsula near Baku in 1846–1848, and in the 20th century rotary drilling largely replaced cable tools, reaching much greater depths in less time.

entries.name: Chicago Pile-1
entries.desc: Chicago Pile-1 (CP-1) was the first artificial nuclear reactor, built under the west stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago, where the first human-made self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction was initiated on 2 December 1942. A team of about 30 led by Enrico Fermi assembled it from natural uranium and ultra-pure graphite blocks, which served as the neutron moderator. It ran at about half a watt, without shielding or cooling, and was the first major technical achievement of the Manhattan Project. In 1943 it was rebuilt near Chicago as Chicago Pile-2.

credit.artist: Melvin A. Miller of the Argonne National Laboratory

entries.name: Solar cell
entries.desc: A solar cell, or photovoltaic cell, is an electronic device that converts the energy of light directly into electricity through the photovoltaic effect; the French physicist Edmond Becquerel built the first in 1839. The first practical photovoltaic cell was publicly demonstrated at Bell Laboratories in 1954, and by the 1960s solar cells were the main power source of most Earth-orbiting satellites. Almost all commercial cells are made of crystalline silicon, and module prices, adjusted for inflation, fell from $96 a watt in the mid-1970s to 30 cents in 2018.

entries.name: Wheel
entries.desc: A wheel is a rotating component, usually circular, that turns on an axle; the oldest indirect evidence of wheeled movement, miniature clay wheels found north of the Black Sea, dates from before 4000 BCE. Pictographs of wheeled wagons at Uruk in Mesopotamia date to c. 3500–3350 BCE, and the wooden Ljubljana Marshes Wheel from Slovenia to 3340–3030 BCE. The spoked wheel, first known from the Sintashta culture c. 2000 BCE, allowed lighter and swifter vehicles such as war chariots.

entries.name: Sail
entries.desc: A sail is a tensile structure of fabric or another membrane that uses the wind to propel a craft; sailing boats appear on Cucuteni–Trypillian ceramics from the 6th millennium BCE, and excavations of the Ubaid period in Mesopotamia give direct evidence of them. When and where the sail was invented is not known. Sails are depicted in Egypt around 3200 BCE, on reed boats sailing up the Nile against its current. Austronesian crab claw sails, used with outriggers and catamarans, carried settlers from Taiwan as far as Polynesia and Madagascar.

entries.name: Domestication of the horse
entries.desc: The domestication of the horse turned wild horses into domestic animals; genomic evidence places the source of all modern domestic horses in the Volga–Don region of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, in present-day southwestern Russia, around 2200 BCE. Earlier claims, notably for the Botai culture of Kazakhstan in 3700–3500 BCE, remain debated. From this core area the domestic lineage spread rapidly across Eurasia for transport, farm work and warfare, replacing other local horse populations. Horses buried with chariots in Sintashta and Petrovka graves of about 2100–1700 BCE give the most persuasive archaeological evidence.

entries.name: Outrigger canoe
entries.desc: An outrigger canoe is a boat steadied by one or more side floats, or outriggers, fastened to its hull; such boats were developed by the Austronesian-speaking peoples of the islands of Southeast Asia, and they enabled the Austronesian expansion from Taiwan from around 3000 BCE. Outrigger and double-hulled canoes carried Austronesians east to Polynesia and New Zealand and west across the Indian Ocean as far as Madagascar. Through early Austronesian contact, estimated at around 1000–600 BCE and later, they spread to Sri Lanka and southern India, and they also reached East Africa.

entries.name: Stirrup
entries.desc: A stirrup is a light frame or ring hung by a strap from a saddle to hold a rider's foot, first known in China under the Jin dynasty in the early 4th century CE. A tomb figurine of 302 shows a mounting stirrup and one of about 322 a riding pair; stirrups appear to have been in widespread use across China by 477. Central Asian invaders such as the Avars brought them to Europe, where they occur in 7th-century Avar graves in Hungary. By steadying the rider, they changed the tactics of mounted warfare.

entries.name: Lateen sail
entries.desc: A lateen is a triangular sail set on a long yard mounted at an angle on the mast and running fore and aft; it originated in the Mediterranean as early as the 2nd century CE, in Roman times. It became common there by the 5th century and by the 6th had largely replaced the square sail, a change suggested to have been made on cost grounds, as the two rigs performed much alike. Arab seafarers adopted it after the Muslim conquests, and it later rigged caravels and the mizzens of full-rigged ships.

entries.name: Sternpost rudder
entries.desc: A sternpost rudder is a steering blade hung at the centre of a ship's stern, first known from pottery models of Chinese junks of the 1st century CE, under the Han dynasty. Unlike the steering oars used earlier, it did not get in the way of the sails, needed less effort from the helmsman and suited larger ocean-going ships. In Europe the oldest known depiction of a pintle-and-gudgeon rudder dates from around 1180, and Joseph Needham held that the stern-mounted rudder reached Europe and the Islamic world from China.

entries.name: Astrolabe
entries.desc: An astrolabe is an astronomical instrument that serves as a star chart and model of the visible sky, used to measure the altitude of stars and find latitude; it dates from classical antiquity, and Theon of Alexandria (c. 335–405) wrote a detailed treatise on it. The earliest extant treatise is that of John Philoponus, of about 550, and the earliest surviving astrolabe is dated 927–928. Muslim astronomers added azimuth scales and used it to fix prayer times and the qibla, and it served European astronomers and navigators into the Age of Discovery.

entries.name: Marine chronometer
entries.desc: A marine chronometer is a precision timepiece carried on a ship to find its longitude by comparing Greenwich Mean Time with local time, first developed in the 18th century: the Yorkshire carpenter John Harrison's H4 of 1761 solved the precision problems of keeping time at sea. Harrison submitted it for the £20,000 longitude prize that the British government had offered in 1714. Pierre Le Roy's detent escapement and the simplified escapements of Thomas Earnshaw and John Arnold shaped later instruments, which the Royal Navy was supplying routinely to its ships by 1825.

entries.name: Steam locomotive
entries.desc: A steam locomotive is a self-propelled steam engine on wheels that moves itself and other vehicles by expanding steam; it was first developed in the United Kingdom, where on 21 February 1804 one of Richard Trevithick's locomotives made the first recorded steam-hauled railway journey, at Pen-y-darren in South Wales. George Stephenson's Locomotion No. 1 hauled passengers on the public Stockton and Darlington Railway in 1825, and the success of Rocket at the Rainhill Trials of 1829 opened the way to inter-city railways. From the early 1900s electric and diesel locomotives gradually replaced steam.

entries.name: Bicycle
entries.desc: A bicycle is a pedal-driven, single-track vehicle with two wheels attached to a frame, one behind the other. Its first form, Karl von Drais’s two-wheeled running machine without pedals, was shown in Mannheim in 1817, and pedals on an enlarged front wheel were added in France in the early 1860s. The upright safety bicycle has changed little since the first chain-driven model of around 1885, and it gave women unprecedented mobility. Ball bearings, pneumatic tyres, chain-driven sprockets and tension-spoked wheels were first invented for the bicycle.

credit.artist: Karen Roe from Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, UK, United Kingdom

entries.name: Automobile
entries.desc: An automobile, or car, is a wheeled motor vehicle that runs mainly on roads; the modern car was invented in 1886, when the German inventor Carl Benz patented his Benz Patent-Motorwagen. It followed steam road vehicles, beginning with Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot's full-scale steam vehicle of about 1769, and early internal-combustion vehicles that did not succeed. Large-scale production began with Ransom Olds in 1901 and was greatly expanded by Henry Ford's moving assembly line of 1913; by 2025 more than 1.6 billion cars were in use.

entries.name: Aeroplane
entries.desc: An aeroplane is a fixed-wing aircraft driven forward by the thrust of a propeller, jet engine or rocket engine; the Wright brothers invented and flew the Wright Flyer in 1903, in what is recognised as the first sustained and controlled heavier-than-air powered flight. They built on George Cayley's concept of 1799 and on the gliding flights of Otto Lilienthal. Aeroplanes served in the First World War and in every major battle of the Second, the first jet aircraft flew in 1939, and commercial aviation now carries more than four billion passengers a year.

entries.name: Rocket
entries.desc: A rocket is an elongated flying vehicle driven by a rocket engine, carrying all its propellant and so needing no surrounding air; gunpowder rockets evolved in China under the Song dynasty by the 13th century. The Mongols spread them to the Middle East and Europe, and the iron-cased rockets of Mysore were the model for Britain's Congreve rocket of 1804. Modern rockets date from 1926, when Robert Goddard fitted a supersonic nozzle to a high-pressure combustion chamber, and in 1944 the German V-2 became the first artificial object to travel into space.

entries.name: Jet engine
entries.desc: A jet engine is a reaction engine that discharges a fast-moving jet of heated gas to produce thrust; the first patent for using a gas turbine to power an aircraft was filed in 1921 by Maxime Guillaume, though his engine was never built. Frank Whittle applied for a turbojet patent in England in 1930, and in Germany Hans von Ohain, at first unaware of Whittle's work, developed the engine of the Heinkel He 178, the world's first jet plane, which flew in August 1939. By the 1960s all large civilian aircraft were jet-powered.

entries.name: Trireme
entries.desc: The trireme was an ancient Mediterranean galley driven by three banks of oars with one man to each oar, first referred to at the end of the 8th century BCE; scholars are divided on whether it came from Greece or Phoenicia. Fast and agile, with a crew of about 200 including 170 rowers, it was the dominant warship of the Mediterranean from the 7th to the 4th centuries BCE. Triremes played a vital role in the Persian Wars, and a fleet of over 200 was the foundation of Athenian power.

entries.name: Fire lance
entries.desc: The fire lance was an early gunpowder weapon: a tube of gunpowder, usually bamboo, strapped to a spear or other polearm, with the earliest evidence from China in 950. Its first recorded use in war came in 1132, when Song garrisons used fire lances at the siege of De'an against the Jin. Pellets and shards were later added to the charge, and by the late 13th century metal barrels used without the lance had become the first hand cannons, making it the ancestor of modern firearms.

entries.name: Cannon
entries.desc: A cannon is a large-calibre gun, a type of artillery firing a projectile with an explosive propellant, first securely attested in China in the 13th century. It probably developed from or alongside the fire lance: Yuan troops are recorded using hand cannons in 1288, and the Xanadu Gun of 1298 is the earliest extant cannon with a date of production. Gunpowder was its main propellant until the late 19th century; by the end of the 14th century cannons were widespread across Eurasia, and in 1453 Ottoman bombards broke the walls of Constantinople.

entries.name: Hwacha
entries.desc: The hwacha was a Korean weapons platform, a wooden cart carrying a launch pad, first built in 1409 under the Joseon dynasty; it could fire up to 200 rocket-powered arrows, or volleys of arrows and bolts from gun barrels. It was developed from the juhwa and the singijeon, Korean rockets and rocket-powered arrows. Hundreds were deployed across Korea by the end of 1451, and in the Japanese invasions of 1592–1598 forty hwachas helped 3,400 Koreans repel 30,000 Japanese at the Battle of Haengju.

entries.name: Turtle ship
entries.desc: The turtle ship (geobukseon) was a Korean warship named after its covering, said to resemble a turtle's shell, and first recorded in 1413 in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty. Its roof was covered with iron spikes against boarding, it was driven by both oars and sails, and it carried several types of cannon and a dragon's head at the bow. Admiral Yi Sun-sin, credited with designing an improved version, used turtle ships against the Japanese invasions of 1592–1598; whether they were armoured with iron plates is disputed.

entries.name: Submarine
entries.desc: A submarine is a watercraft capable of independent operation underwater; the first submersible of which reliable information exists, propelled by oars, was built in 1620 by Cornelis Drebbel, a Dutchman in the service of James I of England. The first verified submarine able to operate and move independently underwater was David Bushnell's one-man Turtle of 1775, also the first military submersible. Navies could put submarines into routine service only once suitable engines were developed, in the late 19th century, and they were first used widely in the First World War.

credit.artist: U.S. Navy photo by General Dynamics Electric Boat

entries.name: Tank
entries.desc: A tank is an armoured fighting vehicle combining heavy firepower, strong armour and the mobility of tracks and a powerful engine; the first British prototype, Little Willie, was built at William Foster & Co. in Lincoln, England, in 1915. Britain and France developed tanks separately and at the same time to break the deadlock of trench warfare in the First World War; no single inventor can be named, though Walter Gordon Wilson and William Tritton played leading roles. The British Mark I first went into battle at the Somme in September 1916.

entries.name: Ishango bone
entries.desc: The Ishango bone is an engraved bone tool found at Ishango, near the Semliki River in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and believed to be about 20,000 years old. About 10 centimetres long, with a sharp piece of quartz fixed to one end, it bears 168 marks in three columns, read as tallies, a counting tool or a lunar calendar. Its dating and meaning are both debated. It was found in 1950 by the Belgian Jean de Heinzelin de Braucourt, who took it to the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences in Brussels.

entries.name: Clay tokens
entries.desc: Clay tokens are small shaped pieces of clay that stood for animals and goods, first used to keep records in the ancient Near East around 8000–7500 BCE; the earliest known come from the Zagros region of Iran. For trade they were sealed in hollow clay balls, or bullae, to prevent deception. Marks impressed and later drawn on clay tablets replaced them, and around 3100 BCE, when signs for numbers appeared, the tokens gave way to pictographic tablets, the beginning of Sumerian cuneiform.

entries.name: Sexagesimal
entries.desc: Sexagesimal, or base 60, is a numeral system with sixty as its base, which originated with the Sumerians in the 3rd millennium BCE and passed to the Babylonians. In Mesopotamia it was written with cuneiform signs, using ten as a sub-base, and at first had no symbol for zero, so a number's value sometimes had to be judged from its context. Its twelve divisors simplify many fractions, and it survives in the 60 minutes of an hour and the 360 degrees of a circle.

entries.name: Abacus
entries.desc: An abacus, or counting frame, is a hand-operated calculating tool of beads or counters moved on a board or rods, first known in Sumer, where it appeared between 2700 and 2300 BCE with columns for the orders of magnitude of the base-60 number system. The marble Salamis Tablet of 300 BCE is the oldest counting board yet discovered. Greek, Roman and Chinese forms followed, and abacuses remained in everyday use until handheld electronic calculators largely replaced them in the 1980s.

entries.name: Proto-Sinaitic script
entries.desc: The Proto-Sinaitic script is the earliest known trace of alphabetic writing, found in about 30–40 inscriptions at Serabit el-Khadim in Sinai and in two at Wadi el-Hol in Middle Egypt dated to between 1900 and 1800 BCE. By the common theory, speakers of a Canaanite language made it from Egyptian hieroglyphs, using the sign for 'house' to write b, the first consonant of the Semitic baytu. Its dating is debated; it is the common ancestor of the Phoenician, Paleo-Hebrew and Ancient South Arabian scripts.

entries.name: Oracle bone script
entries.desc: The oracle bone script is the oldest attested form of written Chinese, carved mostly on ox shoulder bones and turtle plastrons for the Late Shang royal family from the 13th century BCE; inscriptions of King Wu Ding's reign are radiocarbon dated to 1254–1197 BCE. Most of the estimated 150,000 inscriptions, found at Yinxu, the last Shang capital, near modern Anyang, record divinations. Already a mature system, with phonetic loans and phono-semantic compounds, it is the direct ancestor of the later Chinese scripts.

entries.name: Greek alphabet
entries.desc: The Greek alphabet is the script of the Greek language, in use since the late 9th or early 8th century BCE (conventionally about 800 BCE), with early samples from at least 775 BCE. Adapted from the Phoenician alphabet, it turned some Phoenician consonant letters into vowels and so became the earliest known alphabet to write vowels as well as consonants systematically. Local variants gave way by the end of the 4th century BCE to the 24-letter Ionian alphabet, still used today; its western form was the ancestor of the Latin alphabet.

entries.name: Brahmi script
entries.desc: Brahmi is a writing system of ancient India that appeared as a fully developed script in the 3rd century BCE; its earliest securely dated inscriptions are the rock-cut edicts of Ashoka, from 250–232 BCE. It is an abugida, marking vowels with signs attached to consonants. Its origin is much debated: most scholars derive it from, or see the influence of, a Semitic script such as Aramaic. Deciphered by James Prinsep in the 1830s, it is the ancestor of the Brahmic scripts still used across South and Southeast Asia.

entries.name: Maya script
entries.desc: Maya script, or Maya glyphs, is the writing system of the Maya civilisation of Mesoamerica, known from inscriptions of the 3rd century BCE at late Preclassic sites such as San Bartolo in Guatemala and Chakjobon in Mexico. It combined logograms with syllabic signs and was painted on pottery, walls and bark-paper codices or carved in stone and wood. Used until the Spanish conquest, it is the only Mesoamerican script substantially deciphered: over 90 per cent of texts can now be read with reasonable accuracy, after work by Yuri Knorozov and others.

entries.name: Codex
entries.desc: A codex is a book of pages stacked and bound at one edge, the ancestor of the modern book, first described in the 1st century CE, when the Roman poet Martial praised its convenience. The ancient Romans developed it from wax tablets, and early codices were mostly of papyrus, later of parchment. Early Christians favoured it from the 2nd century; the codex equalled the scroll in number around 300 CE and had replaced it across the Christianised Greco-Roman world by the 6th century.

entries.name: Euclid's Elements
entries.desc: Euclid's Elements is a mathematical treatise in 13 books written about 300 BCE by the Greek mathematician Euclid, the oldest surviving large-scale deductive treatment of mathematics. From definitions, postulates and common notions it proves theorems of plane and solid geometry and number theory, among them the Pythagorean theorem and the infinity of the primes. Translated into Arabic and Latin in the Middle Ages and first printed in 1482, it has been called the most successful textbook ever written; Greek manuscripts survive in the Vatican Library and the Bodleian Library.

credit.artist: University of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology

entries.name: Zero
entries.desc: Zero is the number for an empty quantity and the placeholder digit of positional notation, which in its modern use derives from India, where a Jain text internally dated to 458 CE uses a decimal place-value system including zero. Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero in the 7th century, and Islamic mathematicians, among them al-Khwarizmi, transmitted it to Europe, where Fibonacci popularised it. Mesoamerica used zero independently, in Long Count dates from 36 BCE.

entries.name: Quipu
entries.desc: A quipu, or khipu, is a record-keeping device of knotted cords of cotton or camelid fibre, first undisputedly attested in the central Andes in the Middle Horizon, c. 600–1000 CE, when it was probably used by the Wari Empire. The Inca stored numbers in its knots in a decimal positional system and used quipus for taxes, censuses and the calendar. How quipus recorded non-numeric information remains undeciphered and disputed; just under 1,400 pre-Columbian examples are known.

entries.name: Logarithm
entries.desc: A logarithm is the exponent to which a fixed number, the base, must be raised to produce a given number; logarithms were introduced by John Napier in 1614, in his book Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio, as a means of simplifying calculations. With logarithm tables, multi-digit multiplication could be replaced by table look-ups and simpler addition, and navigators, scientists, engineers and surveyors rapidly adopted them. Henry Briggs's table of 1617 introduced 10 as the base, and the slide rule, also based on logarithms, remained an essential calculating tool until the 1970s.

entries.name: Calculus
entries.desc: Calculus is the branch of mathematics that studies continuous change, formulated independently by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in 17th-century Europe. Its two branches, differential and integral calculus, study rates of change and the accumulation of quantities. Newton derived his results in 1665–1666, but Leibniz published first, in 1684, and the dispute over credit divided English-speaking from continental European mathematicians for many years. Newton applied its methods to planetary motion in his Principia (1687), while much of the notation still in use comes from Leibniz.

entries.name: Heliocentrism
entries.desc: Heliocentrism is a superseded astronomical model that placed the Sun at the centre of the universe, with the Earth and the planets orbiting it; the first person known to have proposed it was Aristarchus of Samos, c. 270 BCE. His writings on it are lost, but his contemporary Archimedes described the theory in The Sand Reckoner. Nicolaus Copernicus turned it from philosophical speculation into predictive geometrical astronomy in De revolutionibus, first printed in Nuremberg in 1543, and between 1617 and 1621 Johannes Kepler gave all the planets elliptical orbits around the Sun.

entries.name: Antikythera mechanism
entries.desc: The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery, a geared model of the Solar System, built in the 2nd century BCE and recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera. The oldest known example of an analogue computer, it could predict astronomical positions and eclipses decades in advance and track the four-year cycle of the ancient Olympic Games. Scans made in 2005 suggest that it had 35 meshing bronze gears. Its 82 fragments are kept at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

entries.name: Book of Optics
entries.desc: The Book of Optics is a seven-volume treatise on optics written between 1011 and 1021 by the medieval Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham, known in the West as Alhazen (965–c. 1040). It argues on experimental grounds against the extramission theory of vision held by Euclid and Ptolemy, and proposes that sight takes place by light entering the eye, the model accepted today. It also describes the camera obscura. Translated into Latin around 1200 and printed by Friedrich Risner in 1572, it strongly influenced European optics, physics and mathematics between the 13th and 17th centuries.

entries.name: Camera obscura
entries.desc: A camera obscura is a dark chamber or box in which light passing through a small hole projects an inverted image of the scene outside onto the opposite surface; one of the earliest known written records of the effect is the Chinese text Mozi, of the 4th century BCE. Ibn al-Haytham studied it extensively in the early 11th century. Fitted with a lens from the second half of the 16th century, it became a popular drawing aid, and in the first half of the 19th century it developed into the photographic camera.

entries.name: Telescope
entries.desc: A telescope is an instrument for observing distant objects by the radiation they emit, absorb or reflect; the first known practical telescopes, refractors with glass lenses, were invented in the Netherlands at the beginning of the 17th century. The earliest record of one is a patent application of 1608 by the Middelburg spectacle maker Hans Lipperhey, though the actual inventor is unknown. Galileo built his own version in 1609 and used it to observe celestial objects, and Isaac Newton built the first practical reflecting telescope in 1668.

entries.name: Microscope
entries.desc: A microscope is an instrument for examining objects too small to be seen by the naked eye; the earliest known compound microscopes, which combine an objective lens near the specimen with an eyepiece, appeared in Europe around 1620. The inventor is unknown, and claims have been made for spectacle makers in the Netherlands and for Cornelis Drebbel. It remained largely a novelty until the 1660s and 1670s, when naturalists in Italy, the Netherlands and England began using it to study biology; Antonie van Leeuwenhoek reported the discovery of micro-organisms in 1676.

entries.name: Pendulum clock
entries.desc: A pendulum clock is a clock that uses a swinging weight, the pendulum, as its timekeeping element; it was invented on 25 December 1656 by the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens, inspired by Galileo Galilei's investigations of pendulums, and patented the following year. The pendulum improved the accuracy of clocks from about 15 minutes to 15 seconds a day, and many existing verge-and-foliot clocks were fitted with one. Pendulum clocks remained the world standard for accurate timekeeping until the invention of the quartz clock in 1927.

entries.name: Voltaic pile
entries.desc: The voltaic pile is a stack of paired metal discs separated by brine-soaked cloth or cardboard, the first electrical battery that could continuously provide an electric current; it was invented by the Italian chemist Alessandro Volta, who published his experiments in 1799 and described the device to the Royal Society in London on 20 March 1800. It soon enabled the electrolysis of water, in 1800, and Humphry Davy's isolation of sodium and potassium in 1807. Batteries related to Volta's powered the 19th-century electrical industry until the dynamo arrived in the 1870s.

entries.name: Electromagnetic induction
entries.desc: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force across an electrical conductor in a changing magnetic field; Michael Faraday is generally credited with its discovery, first demonstrated on 29 August 1831 with two wires wound on an iron ring, and Joseph Henry discovered it independently in 1832. Within two months Faraday generated a steady current by rotating a copper disc near a magnet. James Clerk Maxwell later described it mathematically, and it is used in transformers, electric motors and generators.

entries.name: Periodic table
entries.desc: The periodic table is an ordered arrangement of the chemical elements into rows (periods) and columns (groups), in which elements of the same group tend to show similar chemical properties; the first to become generally accepted was that of the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev, published in 1869. He left gaps for elements not yet known and predicted the properties of three of them; gallium, scandium and germanium, discovered between 1875 and 1886, matched his predictions. The periodic law it depicts was explained early in the 20th century by the discovery of atomic numbers.

entries.name: Germ theory of disease
entries.desc: The germ theory of disease is the scientific theory that microorganisms, known as pathogens or germs, can cause disease; Athanasius Kircher was the first to attribute infectious disease to a microscopic pathogen, in his Scrutinium Physico-Medicum, published in Rome in 1658. Basic forms of the theory had been proposed by Girolamo Fracastoro in 1546. It took hold only towards the end of the 19th century, replacing the miasma theory that diseases came from bad air, after the work of Louis Pasteur from the late 1850s and of Robert Koch in the 1880s.

entries.name: Mendelian inheritance
entries.desc: Mendelian inheritance is a type of biological inheritance following the principles first derived by Gregor Johann Mendel, a Moravian monk, from experiments with some 28,000 pea plants grown between 1856 and 1863 in his monastery garden; he presented them to the Natural History Society of Brno (Brünn) in 1865 and published them in 1866. Largely ignored at first, his work was rediscovered in 1900 by Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak. Combined with the chromosome theory of inheritance by Thomas Hunt Morgan in 1915, it became the core of classical genetics.

entries.name: X-ray
entries.desc: An X-ray is a form of high-energy electromagnetic radiation, with a wavelength shorter than ultraviolet rays and longer than gamma rays, discovered by the German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen on 8 November 1895. He named it X-radiation to signify an unknown type of radiation and received the first Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery. Because X-rays pass through living tissue, they were taken up in medicine within weeks: John Hall-Edwards first used them under clinical conditions in Birmingham, England, on 11 January 1896. Being ionising, they can also cause burns and cancer.

entries.name: Radioactivity
entries.desc: Radioactivity, or radioactive decay, is the process by which an unstable atomic nucleus loses energy by radiation, discovered in 1896 by Henri Becquerel when uranium salts blackened a photographic plate wrapped in black paper. Marie Curie showed that the rays were a property of atoms; with Pierre Curie she coined the term "radioactivity" and isolated polonium and radium. Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy were the first to realise that many decay processes turn one element into another. Decay is used to estimate the ages of rocks and organic matter.

entries.name: Theory of relativity
entries.desc: The theory of relativity comprises two theories of physics by Albert Einstein: special relativity, published in 1905, and general relativity, a theory of gravitation he developed between 1907 and 1915. Special relativity, introduced in the paper "On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies", holds that light in a vacuum has the same speed for all observers and that mass and energy are equivalent (E = mc²). General relativity explains gravity through curved spacetime. The theories superseded Newton's mechanics, and satellite navigation systems such as GPS must allow for their effects.

entries.name: Quantum mechanics
entries.desc: Quantum mechanics is the physical theory that describes the behaviour of matter and light at and below the scale of atoms; it arose from early theories such as Max Planck's hypothesis of 1900 that energy is radiated and absorbed in discrete "quanta". Albert Einstein used the idea in 1905 to explain the photoelectric effect, and modern quantum mechanics was born in 1925, when Werner Heisenberg, Max Born and Pascual Jordan developed matrix mechanics and Erwin Schrödinger invented wave mechanics. Its applications include the laser, the transistor and magnetic resonance imaging.

entries.name: Atomic theory
entries.desc: Atomic theory is the scientific theory that matter is composed of particles called atoms, set out in its modern form by John Dalton, who explained it to Thomas Thomson in 1804 and published his own version in 1808. The idea of indivisible particles appeared in many ancient cultures, but as philosophy rather than science. Dalton held that all atoms of an element have the same weight, that atoms of different elements differ in weight, and that none are created or destroyed in chemical reactions. Physicists later found that atoms have an inner structure.

entries.name: DNA double helix
entries.desc: The DNA double helix is the structure of double-stranded DNA, two strands wound around each other and held together by paired bases; James Watson and Francis Crick first published the model in the journal Nature in 1953. Their model drew on the work of Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling, whose X-ray diffraction image "Photo 51" was crucial, of Maurice Wilkins and others, and on Erwin Chargaff's base-pairing data. It explained how genetic information is stored and copied, and Crick, Watson and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
